{{confuse|monotonic matrix}}{{One source|date=May 2024}}{{Other use|SMAWK algorithm|Monge array}}
A real square matrix <math>A</math> is '''monotone''' (in the sense of [[Collatz]]) if for all real vectors <math>v</math>, <math>Av \geq 0</math> implies <math>v \geq 0</math>, where <math>\geq</math> is the element-wise order on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>.<ref name="Mangasarian1968">{{cite journal|last1=Mangasarian|first1=O. L.|title=Characterizations of Real Matrices of Monotone Kind|journal=SIAM Review|volume=10|issue=4|year=1968|pages=439–441|issn=0036-1445|doi=10.1137/1010095|bibcode=1968SIAMR..10..439M |url=https://minds.wisconsin.edu/bitstream/handle/1793/57482/TR15.pdf?sequence=1}}</ref>

==Properties==

A monotone matrix is nonsingular.<ref name="Mangasarian1968" />

''Proof'': Let <math>A</math> be a monotone matrix and assume there exists <math>x \ne 0</math> with <math>Ax = 0</math>. Then, by monotonicity, <math>x \geq 0</math> and <math>-x \geq 0</math>, and hence <math>x = 0</math>. <math>\square</math>

Let <math>A</math> be a real square matrix. <math>A</math> is monotone if and only if <math>A^{-1} \geq 0</math>.<ref name="Mangasarian1968" />

''Proof'': Suppose <math>A</math> is monotone. Denote by <math>x</math> the <math>i</math>-th column of <math>A^{-1}</math>. Then, <math>Ax</math> is the <math>i</math>-th standard basis vector, and hence <math>x \geq 0</math> by monotonicity. For the reverse direction, suppose <math>A</math> admits an inverse such that <math>A^{-1} \geq 0</math>. Then, if <math>Ax \geq 0</math>, <math>x = A^{-1} Ax \geq A^{-1} 0 = 0</math>, and hence <math>A</math> is monotone. <math>\square</math>

==Examples==

The matrix <math>\left( \begin{smallmatrix} 1&-2\\ 0&1 \end{smallmatrix} \right)</math> is monotone, with inverse <math>\left( \begin{smallmatrix} 1&2\\ 0&1 \end{smallmatrix} \right)</math>.
In fact, this matrix is an [[M-matrix]] (i.e., a monotone [[L-matrix]]).

Note, however, that not all monotone matrices are M-matrices. An example is <math>\left( \begin{smallmatrix} -1&3\\ 2&-4 \end{smallmatrix} \right)</math>, whose inverse is <math>\left( \begin{smallmatrix} 2&3/2\\ 1&1/2 \end{smallmatrix} \right)</math>.
